newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine Navy admits "Blond Angel" still serving.
newsitem.headline: Argentine Navy admits "Blond Angel" still serving.

text.p: The Argentine Navy admitted on Tuesday that an officer wanted in France and Sweden for human rights crimes who supposedly retired from the military last year still has a role in naval intelligence.
Capt. Alfredo Astiz, known as the "Blond Angel," became a hated symbol of military immunity from punishment for murder, kidnapping and torture under the 1976-83 dictatorship.

Tried and sentenced after democracy returned, but freed under an amnesty for "Dirty War" officers in 1989, he was forced to retire from the Navy late last year after a campaign by human rights groups.
But Pagina 12 newspaper reported under the headline "He's Back" -- and Navy chief Adm. Carlos Marron admitted -- Astiz still carries out duties for the Navy Intelligence Service.

Marron told reporters he "carries out functions to do with foreign and domestic military intelligence" and a Navy spokesman told Reuters Astiz "has been called on from time to time, since he retired, to give his opinion."

Astiz, 46, was sentenced to life in jail in France in absentia for the murder of French nuns Leonie Duquet and Alice Domon in 1977. Sweden wants to try him for the disappearance that year of Swedish teenager Dagmar Hagelin. All three are believed to have been killed at the Navy School of Mechanics (ESMA), the military junta's most infamous torture centre.
Argentina refuses to extradite Astiz, who also walked free from a court-martial for alleged cowardice in the 1982 Falklands War with Britain.

News of his involvement in intelligence-gathering brought angry reaction from Argentina's best-known human rights group, the Mothers of Plaza de Mayo, who campaign for information on people who "disappeared" during the dictatorship.
Officially, the ranks of the "desaparecidos" are estimated to number 10,000, but rights groups put it at 30,000.

Mothers of Plaza de Mayo leader Nora Cortinas spoke of her "disgust at the armed forces and all their accomplices in the government" for letting Astiz retain a role in the services. "After 14 years of constitutional governments we have still not managed to get the repressors to retire," she said.

Graciela Fernandez Meijide, an opposition senator who lost a son in the Dirty War, said the Navy had failed to atone for its crimes, unlike the army, "and they still say that they were just doing their duty."
